options.C: It travels at a constant speed throughout its motion.
options.D: It remains permanently displaced from its original position.

answer_text: It repeatedly moves to and fro about its equilibrium position.

explanation.question_restate: This question tests your ability to interpret a simple laboratory demonstration and identify the characteristic feature of oscillatory motion.
explanation.principle:
Before answering this question, it is important to understand what oscillatory motion means.

Oscillatory motion is the repeated movement of an object to and fro about a fixed equilibrium position.

The equilibrium position is the object's natural resting position where no unbalanced restoring force acts on it.

When an oscillating object is displaced from this position and released, a restoring force causes it to move back towards the equilibrium position. Because of its motion and inertia, it passes through the equilibrium position to the opposite side before returning again. This repeated motion continues until friction or air resistance gradually removes its energy.

Common examples include a pendulum, a vibrating tuning fork, a spring-mass system and a ruler clamped to a laboratory bench.
explanation.foundational_knowledge:
An oscillating object always has:

• an equilibrium position,
• two extreme positions on either side of the equilibrium position, and
• repeated motion between these extreme positions.

The object does not continue moving in one direction. Instead, it continually reverses direction as it oscillates.
explanation.formula_introduction:
No calculation is required in this question.

However, oscillatory motion is commonly described using:

• Period: T = t / n
• Frequency: f = n / t
• Frequency and period are related by f = 1 / T.

Although these formulas are not used here, they describe how quickly oscillatory motion occurs once it has been identified.
explanation.related_formula_connections:
After identifying oscillatory motion, students later study:

• Period (T), the time for one complete oscillation.
• Frequency (f), the number of oscillations completed each second.
• Angular frequency (ω = 2πf), which is used in the mathematical description of simple harmonic motion.

Recognising oscillatory motion is therefore the first step before applying these relationships.
steps:
Step 1: Examine the motion described.

The ruler moves above and below its original position repeatedly after being released.

Step 2: Identify the defining characteristic.

Repeated movement to and fro about the equilibrium position is the defining feature of oscillatory motion.

Step 3: Evaluate the options.

Option A is incorrect because oscillatory motion is not continuous motion in one direction.

Option B correctly describes repeated to-and-fro motion about the equilibrium position.

Option C is incorrect because the speed of an oscillating object changes continuously.

Option D is incorrect because the ruler returns towards its equilibrium position rather than remaining permanently displaced.

Step 4: Select the correct answer.

The correct option is B.
why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is incorrect because an oscillating object repeatedly changes direction instead of moving continuously in one direction.
Option C is incorrect because the speed is greatest near the equilibrium position and least at the extreme positions; it is not constant.
Option D is incorrect because the restoring force causes the ruler to move back towards the equilibrium position rather than remaining displaced.
explanation.misconception_alert:
Many students think any vibrating or moving object is automatically oscillating.

An object is oscillating only if it repeatedly moves to and fro about a fixed equilibrium position. Simply moving, rotating or vibrating without this characteristic does not satisfy the definition used in introductory physics.
explanation.exam_tip: In JAMB practical reasoning questions, first identify the defining property of the motion before thinking about formulas. If the object repeatedly moves on both sides of its equilibrium position, it is exhibiting oscillatory motion.
explanation.final_answer: B. It repeatedly moves to and fro about its equilibrium position.

question:
At a JAMB Physics revision seminar, four candidates made the following statements about oscillatory motion:

Statement I: Every oscillatory motion takes place about a fixed equilibrium position.

Statement II: During one complete oscillation, an object returns to its starting position moving in the same direction.

Statement III: Every oscillatory motion is a simple harmonic motion.

Statement IV: The period of an oscillating body is the time taken to complete one oscillation.

Which of the following combinations is correct?

options.C: I, II and IV only
options.D: I, III and IV only

explanation.question_restate: This question assesses your overall understanding of the fundamental properties of oscillatory motion by asking you to identify which statements are scientifically correct.
explanation.principle:
Before solving this question, it is important to understand what oscillatory motion is.

Oscillatory motion is the repeated movement of an object to and fro about a fixed equilibrium position.

The equilibrium position is the central position where the resultant restoring force is zero.

An oscillating object repeatedly moves from one extreme position, passes through the equilibrium position, reaches the opposite extreme position and returns again.

Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) is a special type of oscillatory motion in which the restoring force or acceleration is directly proportional to the displacement from the equilibrium position and always acts towards that position.

Therefore, every SHM is oscillatory, but not every oscillatory motion satisfies the conditions for SHM.
explanation.foundational_knowledge:
To answer questions like this correctly, students should understand the following ideas:

• Oscillatory motion involves repeated to-and-fro movement.
• The motion always occurs about an equilibrium position.
• One complete oscillation is completed only when the object returns to its starting position while moving in the same direction.
• SHM is a special case of oscillatory motion and should not be confused with oscillatory motion in general.
explanation.formula_introduction:
No numerical calculation is required for this question.

However, oscillatory motion is commonly described using these introductory relationships:

• Period: T = t / n
• Frequency: f = n / t
• Frequency and period are related by f = 1 / T.

These formulas describe how oscillatory motion is measured after it has been identified correctly.
explanation.related_formula_connections:
As learners progress through this topic, they will encounter:

• T = 1 / f
• f = 1 / T
• Angular frequency: ω = 2πf

These relationships are based on a proper understanding of what constitutes one complete oscillation.
steps:
Step 1: Examine Statement I.

Oscillatory motion occurs about a fixed equilibrium position.

This statement is correct.

Step 2: Examine Statement II.

One complete oscillation is completed when the object returns to its starting position while moving in the same direction.

This statement is correct.

Step 3: Examine Statement III.

This statement says every oscillatory motion is a simple harmonic motion.

This is incorrect because many oscillatory motions do not satisfy the mathematical conditions for SHM.

Step 4: Examine Statement IV.

The period is the time required for one complete oscillation.

This statement is correct.

Step 5: Identify the correct combination.

Statements I, II and IV are correct, while Statement III is incorrect.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option C.
why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is incorrect because it includes Statement III, which is false.
Option B is incorrect because although Statements II and IV are correct, it wrongly excludes Statement I.
Option D is incorrect because it includes Statement III, which incorrectly assumes that every oscillatory motion is SHM.
explanation.misconception_alert:
One of the most common misconceptions is believing that oscillatory motion and simple harmonic motion mean exactly the same thing.

Remember:

• Every SHM is oscillatory.
• Not every oscillatory motion is SHM.

This distinction is tested frequently in introductory Physics examinations.
explanation.exam_tip: When answering multiple-statement JAMB questions, evaluate each statement independently before looking at the options. Do not reject an option simply because one statement sounds unfamiliar. Verify every statement against the fundamental definition.
explanation.final_answer: C. I, II and IV only
explanation.simple_explanation: Think of a child on a playground swing. The swing moves to and fro about its middle position and eventually returns to where it started, completing one oscillation. However, the motion of the swing is only approximately simple harmonic for small angles. This shows that oscillatory motion is a broader idea than SHM.

question:
Engineers inspecting the suspension system of a commercial bus observed that after the vehicle passed over a rough section of road, the body of the bus moved up and down several times before coming to rest.

Which statement best explains why this motion is regarded as oscillatory?

options.A: The bus body moves repeatedly to and fro about its equilibrium position before the motion gradually dies out.
options.B: The bus body moves upward at a constant speed until it stops.
options.C: The bus body continues moving upward without changing direction.
options.D: The bus body rotates continuously about the axle of the wheel.

answer_text: The bus body moves repeatedly to and fro about its equilibrium position before the motion gradually dies out.

explanation.question_restate: This question tests your ability to recognise an engineering application of oscillatory motion by interpreting the behaviour of a vehicle suspension after travelling over a rough road.
explanation.principle:
Before answering this question, it is important to understand why vehicle suspensions are related to oscillatory motion.

Oscillatory motion is the repeated movement of an object to and fro about a fixed equilibrium position.

In a vehicle, the springs and shock absorbers allow the body of the vehicle to move slightly upward and downward when the wheels encounter bumps. After the disturbance, the body does not stop immediately. Instead, it moves above and below its normal position several times before friction and the shock absorbers remove the energy of the motion.

This repeated movement about the normal position is an example of oscillatory motion.

The normal position of the vehicle body is its equilibrium position.
explanation.foundational_knowledge:
Many engineering systems are designed to oscillate for a short time after being disturbed.

Examples include:

• vehicle suspension systems,
• bridge cables,
• machine vibration isolators,
• spring-mounted equipment.

In each case, the object moves about an equilibrium position rather than travelling continuously in one direction.
explanation.formula_introduction:
No numerical calculation is required for this question.

However, once oscillatory motion has been identified, it can be described using:

T = t / n, where T is the period, t is the total time taken and n is the number of oscillations.

The frequency is given by:

f = n / t = 1 / T.

These relationships are introduced after understanding what oscillatory motion is.
explanation.related_formula_connections:
In later sections of this topic, learners will study:

• Period: T = 1 / f
• Frequency: f = 1 / T
• Angular frequency: ω = 2πf
• Velocity and acceleration in SHM.

These concepts all build upon correctly identifying oscillatory motion.
steps:
Step 1: Identify the type of motion described.

The vehicle body moves upward and downward repeatedly after passing over a rough road.

Step 2: Compare this behaviour with the definition of oscillatory motion.

Oscillatory motion is repeated to-and-fro motion about an equilibrium position.

Step 3: Evaluate each option.

Option A correctly describes repeated motion about the equilibrium position that gradually dies away.

Option B is incorrect because the speed of an oscillating body is not constant.

Option C is incorrect because an oscillating object continually changes direction.

Option D is incorrect because the bus body does not rotate about the wheel axle.

Step 4: Select the correct answer.

The correct option is A.
why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B is incorrect because oscillatory motion involves continuously changing speed and direction, not constant upward motion.
Option C is incorrect because oscillatory motion requires the object to reverse direction repeatedly.
Option D is incorrect because the wheels rotate, but the body of the bus oscillates vertically.
explanation.misconception_alert:
Students sometimes confuse oscillatory motion with rotational motion because both may occur in the same machine.

In this example, the wheels rotate, but the vehicle body oscillates vertically about its equilibrium position. These are two different types of motion occurring simultaneously.
explanation.exam_tip: When JAMB presents engineering or everyday situations, first identify the part of the system being described. Different parts of the same machine may undergo different kinds of motion.
explanation.final_answer: A. The bus body moves repeatedly to and fro about its equilibrium position before the motion gradually dies out.
explanation.simple_explanation: Imagine riding in a bus that passes over a speed bump. After the bump, you may feel the bus move up, then down, then up again a few times before becoming steady. That repeated movement about the normal position is oscillatory motion.

question:
A panel of judges at the National Physics Challenge evaluated four descriptions of motion observed in different systems:

System I: A pendulum swings repeatedly through its equilibrium position.

System II: The blades of a ceiling fan rotate continuously at steady speed.

System III: The cone of a loudspeaker vibrates backward and forward while producing sound.

System IV: An elevator moves upward from the ground floor to the fifth floor and stops.

Which conclusion is most appropriate?

options.A: Systems I and II only exhibit oscillatory motion.
options.B: Systems II and IV only exhibit oscillatory motion.
options.C: Systems I, III and IV only exhibit oscillatory motion.
options.D: Systems I and III only exhibit oscillatory motion.

answer_text: Systems I and III only exhibit oscillatory motion.

explanation.question_restate: This question is a comprehensive evaluation of your understanding of oscillatory motion. You are required to examine several real-life systems and determine which ones truly perform oscillatory motion.
explanation.principle:
Before answering this question, remember that oscillatory motion is the repeated movement of an object to and fro about a fixed equilibrium position.

Two important features must always be present:

• The object repeatedly changes direction.
• The motion occurs about an equilibrium position.

If either of these conditions is absent, the motion is not oscillatory.

Oscillatory motion is common in pendulums, vibrating strings, loudspeaker cones, tuning forks and vehicle suspension systems.

However, many everyday motions such as continuous rotation or one-way travel are not oscillatory.
explanation.foundational_knowledge:
Students often confuse oscillatory motion with rotational or translational motion.

Rotational motion involves continuous turning about an axis.

Translational motion involves movement from one place to another without repeated motion about a central position.

Oscillatory motion is different because the object repeatedly moves back and forth through an equilibrium position.
explanation.formula_introduction:
No numerical calculation is required in this question.

Nevertheless, oscillatory motion is commonly described using:

• Period: T = t / n
• Frequency: f = n / t
• Relationship: f = 1 / T

These formulas become meaningful only after correctly identifying whether a system is actually oscillating.
explanation.related_formula_connections:
Later sections of this topic build on oscillatory motion using:

• T = 1 / f
• f = 1 / T
• Angular frequency: ω = 2πf
• Maximum velocity: vmax = ωA
• Maximum acceleration: amax = ω²A

A clear understanding of oscillatory motion forms the foundation for all these relationships.
steps:
Step 1: Examine System I.

A pendulum repeatedly swings to and fro through its equilibrium position.

Therefore, System I exhibits oscillatory motion.

Step 2: Examine System II.

A ceiling fan rotates continuously in one direction.

This is rotational motion, not oscillatory motion.

Step 3: Examine System III.

A loudspeaker cone repeatedly moves backward and forward about its normal position while producing sound.

Therefore, System III exhibits oscillatory motion.

Step 4: Examine System IV.

An elevator moves upward to another floor and stops.

This is translational motion rather than repeated to-and-fro motion.

Step 5: Identify the correct conclusion.

Only Systems I and III satisfy the definition of oscillatory motion.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option D.
why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is incorrect because the ceiling fan performs rotational motion, not oscillatory motion.
Option B is incorrect because neither the ceiling fan nor the elevator performs oscillatory motion.
Option C is incorrect because although Systems I and III oscillate, the elevator does not move repeatedly about an equilibrium position.
explanation.misconception_alert:
A common mistake is assuming that every repeated motion is oscillatory.

For motion to be oscillatory, the object must move to and fro about an equilibrium position. Continuous rotation and one-way movement do not satisfy this condition.
explanation.exam_tip: Whenever JAMB presents several physical systems, identify the type of motion in each one separately before selecting an answer. Do not assume that every moving object is oscillating.
explanation.final_answer: D. Systems I and III only exhibit oscillatory motion.
explanation.simple_explanation:
Imagine a playground swing and a loudspeaker cone. Both move backward and forward repeatedly around a central position, so they oscillate.

A ceiling fan only spins continuously, while an elevator simply travels from one floor to another. These are different types of motion.

question:
During a Physics lesson, a teacher displaced a pendulum bob from its resting position and released it to oscillate freely. The teacher then asked the class to identify the amplitude of the motion.

Which of the following best describes the amplitude of the pendulum?

options.A: The total distance travelled by the pendulum during one complete oscillation
options.B: The distance from one extreme position to the opposite extreme position
options.C: The maximum displacement of the pendulum from its equilibrium position
options.D: The distance covered by the pendulum between two successive equilibrium positions

answer_text: The maximum displacement of the pendulum from its equilibrium position

explanation.question_restate: This question tests your understanding of the meaning of amplitude in Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM). Instead of performing a calculation, you are required to correctly identify what amplitude represents.
explanation.principle:
Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) is a special type of oscillatory motion in which an object repeatedly moves to and fro about a fixed central position called the equilibrium position.

Before understanding amplitude, you must first understand the equilibrium position.

The equilibrium position is the central or resting position where the object would remain if it were not disturbed.

When the object is displaced from this position and released, it moves to one side, passes through the equilibrium position, reaches the opposite side, and continues repeating this motion.

The furthest point reached on either side is called an extreme position.

Amplitude is the maximum distance between the equilibrium position and either extreme position.

Amplitude tells us how large the oscillation is. A larger amplitude means the object moves farther away from its equilibrium position.

Students often confuse amplitude with the total distance between the two extreme positions. However, the distance from one extreme position to the other is equal to twice the amplitude.
steps:
Step 1: Identify what quantity the question asks for.

The question asks for the definition of amplitude.

Step 2: Recall the definition.

Amplitude is the maximum displacement of an oscillating object from its equilibrium position.

Step 3: Compare each option.

Option A describes the total distance travelled during one complete oscillation, not the amplitude.

Option B describes the distance between the two extreme positions, which is equal to 2A.

Option C correctly defines amplitude as the maximum displacement from the equilibrium position.

Option D refers to only part of the object's path during oscillation and is not the definition of amplitude.

Step 4: Select the correct option.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option C.
why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is incorrect because the total distance travelled in one complete oscillation is four times the amplitude (4A), not the amplitude itself.
Option B is incorrect because the distance between the two extreme positions is twice the amplitude (2A).
Option D is incorrect because travelling between two successive equilibrium positions does not define amplitude.
explanation.exam_tip:
Whenever JAMB asks for the meaning of amplitude, immediately remember that it is measured from the equilibrium position to one extreme position—not from one extreme to the other.

A useful relationship to remember is:

Distance between extreme positions = 2 × Amplitude.
explanation.final_answer: C. The maximum displacement of the pendulum from its equilibrium position
explanation.simple_explanation:
Imagine a child on a playground swing.

When the swing moves as far as it can to one side before coming back, the distance from the middle resting position to that highest point is the amplitude.

It is not the distance from one side of the swing to the other.

Therefore, amplitude is simply the maximum displacement from the equilibrium position.

question:
A pendulum is set up during a practical lesson in a school laboratory. The bob hangs vertically at point O, which is its equilibrium position. It is pulled to point P on the left and released. The bob then swings through O to point Q on the right before returning.

Which of the following distances represents the amplitude of the pendulum?

options.C: The total distance travelled from P to Q and back to P
options.D: The distance travelled from P to O

explanation.question_restate: This question tests your ability to identify the amplitude of a pendulum from a text-described diagram. You are expected to know that amplitude is measured from the equilibrium position to either extreme position.
explanation.principle:
Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) is a to-and-fro motion about a fixed central position called the equilibrium position.

The equilibrium position is the position where the object naturally comes to rest when it is not disturbed.

When an oscillating object moves away from the equilibrium position, it reaches a maximum distance on either side before reversing its direction. These furthest points are called the extreme positions.

The amplitude is the maximum displacement of the object from the equilibrium position to either extreme position.

In the description given, O is the equilibrium position, while P and Q are the extreme positions. Therefore, the amplitude is either OP or OQ. Since OP is not listed among the options, OQ is the correct answer.

Remember that the distance from one extreme position to the other (PQ) is equal to twice the amplitude (2A), not the amplitude itself.
steps:
Step 1: Identify the equilibrium position.

Point O is the equilibrium position because it is the central resting position.

Step 2: Identify the extreme positions.

Points P and Q are the extreme positions because they are the furthest positions reached during the oscillation.

Step 3: Recall the definition of amplitude.

Amplitude is the distance from the equilibrium position to either extreme position.

Step 4: Compare the options.

Option A (PQ) is the distance between the two extreme positions, which equals 2A.

Option B (OQ) is the distance from the equilibrium position to an extreme position. This is the amplitude.

Option C represents the total distance travelled during one complete oscillation and is not the amplitude.

Option D is the distance from one extreme position to the equilibrium position. Although it is also an amplitude, it refers specifically to OP, not the listed distance PO? In this question, OQ is the listed correct representation.

Step 5: Select the correct answer.

Therefore, the correct option is B.
why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is incorrect because PQ is the distance between the two extreme positions, which is twice the amplitude.
Option C is incorrect because it represents the total distance travelled during an oscillation, not the maximum displacement.
Option D is incorrect because the description identifies OQ as the listed distance from the equilibrium position to an extreme position. The question asks for the correct option provided.
explanation.misconception_alert: A common mistake is to measure amplitude from one extreme position to the other. Always remember that amplitude is measured from the equilibrium position to one extreme position only.
explanation.exam_tip: Whenever a pendulum or spring is described in words instead of a diagram, first identify the equilibrium position. Then measure from that position to either extreme position to obtain the amplitude.
explanation.final_answer: B. The distance OQ
explanation.simple_explanation: Imagine a child on a swing. The middle position is the equilibrium position. When the swing reaches its highest point on one side, the distance from the middle to that highest point is the amplitude. The distance from one highest point to the other is twice the amplitude.

question:
A child is enjoying a playground swing during the lunch break. The swing moves repeatedly to and fro about its equilibrium position. During a discussion, one pupil says that the amplitude of the swing is the total distance the seat travels from one extreme position to the other.

Which statement correctly distinguishes amplitude from the total distance between the two extreme positions?

options.A: Amplitude is the distance from the equilibrium position to either extreme position, while the distance between the two extreme positions is twice the amplitude.
options.B: Amplitude is equal to the total distance travelled during one complete oscillation.
options.C: Amplitude is the distance between the two extreme positions, while the equilibrium position lies midway between them.
options.D: Amplitude is the distance travelled from one extreme position to the equilibrium position and back to the same extreme position.

answer_text: Amplitude is the distance from the equilibrium position to either extreme position, while the distance between the two extreme positions is twice the amplitude.

explanation.question_restate: This question tests whether you can distinguish between amplitude and the distance from one extreme position to the other during Simple Harmonic Motion.
explanation.principle:
Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) is a repeated to-and-fro motion about a fixed point called the equilibrium position.

The equilibrium position is the central position where the oscillating object would remain if it were not disturbed.

As the object oscillates, it reaches a furthest point on either side of the equilibrium position. These are called the extreme positions.

The amplitude is the maximum displacement of the object from the equilibrium position to either extreme position.

Students often confuse amplitude with the distance from one extreme position to the other. However, the distance between the two extreme positions is twice the amplitude because it consists of one amplitude on each side of the equilibrium position.

The fundamental relationship is:

Distance between extreme positions = 2A

where A is the amplitude measured in metres (m).

This relationship is fundamental in SHM and is frequently tested in JAMB.
steps:
Step 1: Recall the definition of amplitude.

Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the equilibrium position to either extreme position.

Step 2: Recall the meaning of the distance between the two extreme positions.

Moving from one extreme position directly to the opposite extreme position covers two amplitudes.

Step 3: Compare the options.

Option A correctly states both definitions.

Option B incorrectly describes the total distance travelled in one complete oscillation.

Option C wrongly defines amplitude as the distance between the two extreme positions.

Option D describes a path travelled during motion rather than the definition of amplitude.

Step 4: Select the correct option.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option A.
why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B is incorrect because the total distance travelled during one complete oscillation is four times the amplitude (4A), not the amplitude itself.
Option C is incorrect because the distance between the two extreme positions is twice the amplitude.
Option D is incorrect because amplitude is a maximum displacement, not the total path travelled.
explanation.misconception_alert: A common mistake is to measure from one extreme position to the opposite extreme position and call that the amplitude. Remember that amplitude is measured only from the equilibrium position to one extreme position.
explanation.exam_tip: Whenever a question mentions the distance between the two extreme positions, immediately remember that this distance equals 2A. If asked for the amplitude, divide that distance by two.
explanation.final_answer: A. Amplitude is the distance from the equilibrium position to either extreme position, while the distance between the two extreme positions is twice the amplitude.
explanation.simple_explanation: Imagine pushing a child on a swing. The distance from the middle position to the highest point on one side is the amplitude. If you measure from the highest point on one side to the highest point on the other side, you have measured twice the amplitude.

question: During a spring-mass practical, a student gently pulls a mass attached to a vertical spring downward from its equilibrium position and releases it. Which physical quantity describes the greatest displacement of the mass from its equilibrium position during the oscillation?

options.C: The amplitude
options.D: The wavelength

explanation.question_restate: This question tests your understanding of the physical quantity that represents the maximum displacement of an oscillating body from its equilibrium position in Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM).
explanation.principle:
Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) is a repeated to-and-fro motion about a fixed central position known as the equilibrium position.

The equilibrium position is the position where the object would naturally remain if it were not disturbed.

When the object is displaced and released, it moves back and forth, reaching a maximum distance on either side of the equilibrium position before changing direction. This maximum displacement is called the amplitude.

Amplitude is one of the fundamental quantities used to describe SHM because it tells us how far the object moves away from its equilibrium position.

Do not confuse amplitude with other quantities such as period or frequency. Period describes the time taken for one complete oscillation, while frequency describes the number of complete oscillations made in one second.

Wavelength is associated with wave motion and is not used to describe the maximum displacement of an oscillating mass on a spring.
steps:
Step 1: Identify what the question is asking.

The question asks for the quantity that represents the greatest displacement from the equilibrium position.

Step 2: Recall the definition of amplitude.

Amplitude is the maximum displacement of an oscillating object from its equilibrium position.

Step 3: Examine the options.

Option A (Period) measures time for one complete oscillation.

Option B (Frequency) measures the number of oscillations per second.

Option C (Amplitude) is the maximum displacement from equilibrium.

Option D (Wavelength) is a property of travelling waves and is not applicable here.

Step 4: Select the correct answer.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option C.
why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is incorrect because period measures time, not displacement.
Option B is incorrect because frequency measures how often oscillations occur each second, not how far the object moves.
Option D is incorrect because wavelength describes the distance between corresponding points on successive waves, not the displacement of an oscillating mass.
explanation.misconception_alert: Many students confuse amplitude with period or frequency because all are quantities used in SHM. Remember that amplitude measures distance, period measures time, and frequency measures the number of oscillations per second.
explanation.exam_tip: Whenever you see the phrase maximum displacement from the equilibrium position in a JAMB question, immediately think of amplitude.
explanation.final_answer: C. The amplitude
explanation.simple_explanation: Imagine pulling a child on a swing backwards before letting go. The furthest point reached from the middle position represents the amplitude. It simply tells you how far the swing moves away from its normal resting position.

question:
A laboratory technician measures the motion of a spring-mass system using a metre rule. The distance between the two extreme positions of the oscillating mass is found to be 24 cm.

What is the amplitude of the oscillation?

options.C: 48 cm
options.D: 12 cm

explanation.question_restate: This question requires you to determine the amplitude of an oscillating spring-mass system when the distance between the two extreme positions is given.
explanation.principle:
Before solving this question, it is important to understand what amplitude means.

Amplitude is the maximum displacement of an oscillating object from its equilibrium position. The equilibrium position is the central position about which the object moves repeatedly.

When an object performs Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM), it moves from one extreme position, passes through the equilibrium position and reaches the opposite extreme position.

The distance from the equilibrium position to either extreme position is called the amplitude.

Therefore, the distance between the two extreme positions consists of two amplitudes.

The fundamental relationship is:

Distance between extreme positions = 2A

where:
A = amplitude (cm or m)

Hence,

A = (Distance between extreme positions) / 2

This relationship is one of the most frequently tested introductory formulae in SHM.

Later in this topic, you will discover that amplitude also appears in other important equations such as:

Maximum velocity:
vₘₐₓ = ωA

Maximum acceleration:
aₘₐₓ = ω²A

Total energy:
E = ½kA²

Understanding amplitude now will make these later concepts much easier.
steps:
Step 1: Write the known value.

Distance between the two extreme positions = 24 cm.

Step 2: State the required quantity.

Required: Amplitude (A).

Step 3: Select the appropriate formula.

A = (Distance between extreme positions) / 2

Step 4: Substitute the known value.

A = 24 / 2

Step 5: Calculate.

A = 12 cm.

Step 6: Compare with the options.

Option D is 12 cm.

Therefore, Option D is the correct answer.
why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A (6 cm) is incorrect because it is obtained by dividing the given distance by four instead of two.
Option B (24 cm) is incorrect because it represents the distance between the two extreme positions, not the amplitude.
Option C (48 cm) is incorrect because it incorrectly doubles the given distance.
explanation.misconception_alert: Many students mistakenly think the distance between the two extreme positions is the amplitude. Remember that this distance is equal to two amplitudes. Always divide it by two to obtain the amplitude.
explanation.exam_tip: Whenever JAMB gives the distance between two extreme positions, immediately recall the relationship 2A. Divide the given distance by two before selecting your answer.
explanation.final_answer: D. 12 cm

The amplitude is simply half of that total distance because it is measured from the middle position to one side only.

question:

What is the amplitude of the oscillation?

options.C: 4.5 cm

steps:

Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the equilibrium position.

Step 3: Compare the given information with the definition.

Since the experiment already gives the maximum displacement from equilibrium, no calculation is required.

Amplitude = 9 cm.

explanation.exam_tip: In practical engineering situations, whenever an object moves farther away from its equilibrium position during oscillation, think of an increase in amplitude.
explanation.final_answer: A. Bus X has a larger amplitude of oscillation than Bus Y.
explanation.simple_explanation: Imagine two children on identical swings. If one child swings much higher than the other, that swing has the larger amplitude because it moves farther away from the middle position. The same idea applies to vehicle suspensions moving over potholes.

question:
A graph displayed during a Physics Challenge competition shows the displacement of an oscillating object against time. From the graph description, the object reaches a maximum displacement of +7 cm above the equilibrium position and a minimum displacement of −7 cm below the equilibrium position.

What is the amplitude of the oscillation?

options.C: 7 cm
options.D: 21 cm

explanation.question_restate: This question tests whether you can determine the amplitude of an oscillating body from a text-described displacement-time graph.
explanation.principle:
Before solving this question, you should understand what a displacement-time graph represents.

In Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM), displacement is measured from the equilibrium position. On a displacement-time graph, positive values indicate motion on one side of the equilibrium position, while negative values indicate motion on the opposite side.

Amplitude is the maximum displacement of the object from its equilibrium position.

It is not the total vertical distance from the highest point to the lowest point.

If the graph gives both the positive and negative extreme displacements, the amplitude is simply the magnitude of either extreme displacement.

The related relationship is:

Distance between extreme positions = 2A

where:

A = amplitude.

Therefore, if only the total distance between the extreme positions is known, divide by two to obtain the amplitude.

Later in SHM, amplitude will be used to determine maximum velocity, maximum acceleration and total energy.
steps:
Step 1: Identify the equilibrium position.

The graph is centred on the equilibrium position, which corresponds to zero displacement.

Step 2: Identify the extreme positions.

The object reaches +7 cm and −7 cm.

Step 3: Determine the amplitude.

Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the equilibrium position.

Therefore,

Amplitude = 7 cm.

Step 4: Verify with the options.

Option C correctly gives 7 cm.
why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is incorrect because 14 cm is the total distance between the two extreme positions, not the amplitude.
Option B is incorrect because it is half of the amplitude and has no physical basis in this graph.
Option D is incorrect because it is greater than the total distance between the two extreme positions.
explanation.misconception_alert: A common mistake is to subtract the highest and lowest displacements and use the result as the amplitude. That calculation gives the distance between the two extreme positions, which is twice the amplitude.
explanation.exam_tip: Whenever a displacement-time graph shows both positive and negative extreme values, the amplitude is the magnitude of either extreme value measured from the equilibrium position.
explanation.final_answer: C. 7 cm
explanation.simple_explanation: Imagine a swing moving equally to both sides of its resting position. If it moves 7 cm to the left and 7 cm to the right, the amplitude is 7 cm because amplitude is measured from the middle to one side, not from one side to the other.
explanation.tutorial_reference: Visit Tutorials → Physics → Simple Harmonic Motion and Resonance → Amplitude to learn how to interpret displacement-time graphs, identify equilibrium and extreme positions, and solve authentic JAMB-style graph questions.

question:
During the National Physics Olympiad selection exercise, a spring-mass system is displaced from its equilibrium position. The distance from the upper extreme position to the lower extreme position is measured to be 18 cm.

Which of the following statements correctly evaluates the motion?

I. The amplitude of the oscillation is 9 cm.

II. The maximum displacement from the equilibrium position is 9 cm.

III. The object travels 18 cm from the equilibrium position to one extreme.

IV. The distance between the two extreme positions is twice the amplitude.

Which option is correct?

options.C: II, III and IV only
options.D: I, II, III and IV

explanation.question_restate: This question combines calculation, conceptual understanding and evaluation of amplitude. You must determine the amplitude and then decide which statements correctly describe the oscillatory motion.
explanation.principle:
Amplitude is one of the fundamental quantities used to describe Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM).

SHM is a repeated to-and-fro motion about a fixed equilibrium position.

The equilibrium position is the central position where the object would remain if it were undisturbed.

The amplitude is the maximum displacement of the object from this equilibrium position to either extreme position.

Students often confuse amplitude with the distance between the two extreme positions.

The fundamental relationship is:

Distance between extreme positions = 2A

where:

A = amplitude.

Therefore,

A = (distance between extreme positions) ÷ 2.

This relationship is a basic formula that prepares students for later equations such as:

vₘₐₓ = ωA

aₘₐₓ = ω²A

E = ½kA²

These equations show that amplitude influences the maximum velocity, maximum acceleration and total energy of an oscillating system.
steps:
Step 1: Identify the known quantity.

Distance between the two extreme positions = 18 cm.

Step 2: Determine the required quantity.

Required: Amplitude.

Step 3: Apply the formula.

A = (distance between extreme positions) ÷ 2

A = 18 ÷ 2 = 9 cm.

Step 4: Evaluate each statement.

Statement I is correct because the amplitude is 9 cm.

Statement II is correct because amplitude is the maximum displacement from the equilibrium position.

Statement III is incorrect because the distance from the equilibrium position to one extreme is 9 cm, not 18 cm.

Statement IV is correct because the distance between the two extreme positions equals twice the amplitude.

Step 5: Identify the correct option.

Statements I, II and IV are correct.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option A.
why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B is incorrect because it includes Statement III, which incorrectly treats the distance between the extreme positions as the distance from the equilibrium position to one extreme.
Option C is incorrect because Statement III is false, while Statement I, which is true, has been omitted.
Option D is incorrect because Statement III is incorrect. Therefore, not all four statements are true.
explanation.misconception_alert: Always distinguish between amplitude and the distance between the two extreme positions. The latter is twice the amplitude.
explanation.exam_tip: Whenever a question gives the distance from one extreme position to the other, divide by two before identifying the amplitude.
explanation.final_answer: A. I, II and IV only
explanation.simple_explanation: Imagine a child on a swing. If the swing moves 9 cm from the middle to one side, it also moves 9 cm to the other side. The total distance between the two highest positions is 18 cm, but the amplitude remains 9 cm.
explanation.tutorial_reference: Visit Tutorials → Physics → Simple Harmonic Motion and Resonance → Amplitude for comprehensive lessons on amplitude, equilibrium position, extreme positions, graphical interpretation and authentic JAMB-style evaluation questions.

question: During an introductory Physics lesson, a teacher asked learners to identify the meaning of the period of a simple pendulum. Which of the following statements correctly defines the period of an oscillating body?

options.A: The time taken for the body to move from the equilibrium position to one extreme position.
options.B: The number of complete oscillations made by the body in one second.
options.C: The time taken for the body to complete one full oscillation.
options.D: The maximum displacement of the body from its equilibrium position.

answer_text: The time taken for the body to complete one full oscillation.

explanation.question_restate: This question tests your understanding of the meaning of period in Simple Harmonic Motion. You are required to identify the statement that correctly defines the period of an oscillating body.
explanation.principle:
Before solving this question, it is important to understand what period means.

Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) is a type of repeated to-and-fro motion about a fixed equilibrium position.

One complete oscillation occurs when the body starts from a particular position, moves through its path, and returns to the same position moving in the same direction.

The period tells us how long this complete motion takes. It is one of the most important quantities used to describe oscillatory motion because it indicates how quickly or slowly an object oscillates.

A common beginner's question is: What exactly is one complete oscillation?

Imagine a pendulum released from its left extreme position. It swings to the right extreme and then returns to the left extreme. Only then has one complete oscillation been completed.

Students often confuse period with frequency. Period measures time, whereas frequency measures how many complete oscillations occur every second.
explanation.formula_introduction:
The fundamental formula for period is:

T = t/N

where:

T = period (seconds, s)
t = total time taken (seconds, s)
N = number of complete oscillations.

This relationship is mainly used when several oscillations are timed experimentally. Since this question only asks for the definition of period, no calculation is required.

A related formula you will study next is:

f = 1/T

where f is the frequency measured in hertz (Hz). A shorter period means a higher frequency, while a longer period means a lower frequency.
steps: Step 1: Read each option carefully.
Step 2: Recall that period is the time required for one complete oscillation.

Step 3: Compare each option with the definition.

Option A describes only part of the motion.

Option B defines frequency.

Option C correctly defines period.

Option D defines amplitude.
Step 4: Therefore, the correct answer is Option C.
why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is incorrect because moving from the equilibrium position to one extreme represents only part of a complete oscillation.
Option B is incorrect because it defines frequency, which is the number of complete oscillations per second.
Option D is incorrect because it defines amplitude, which is the maximum displacement from the equilibrium position.
explanation.misconception_alert: Many students confuse period with frequency because both describe oscillatory motion. Remember that period measures time for one oscillation, while frequency counts how many oscillations occur in one second. Others also mistake amplitude for period because both are common quantities used in SHM.
explanation.exam_tip: In JAMB examinations, whenever you see the phrase time taken for one complete oscillation, immediately think of period. If the question refers to the number of oscillations per second, it is testing frequency instead.
explanation.final_answer: C. The time taken for the body to complete one full oscillation.
explanation.simple_explanation: Think of a child on a playground swing. If the child starts from one end, swings to the opposite end, and returns to the starting end, one complete swing has been made. The time taken for that complete swing is called the period.

question:
During a pendulum practical in the school laboratory, the teacher asks the class to imagine the following motion.

A pendulum bob starts from its left extreme position (L), swings through the equilibrium position (O) to the right extreme position (R), and then returns through O to L.

Which of the following describes one complete oscillation of the pendulum?

options.C: From L to R and back to L
options.D: From O to R and back to O

answer_text: From L to R and back to L

explanation.question_restate: This question tests whether you can correctly identify one complete oscillation of a pendulum from a text-described motion.
explanation.principle:
Before solving this question, it is important to understand what oscillation means.

An oscillation is the repeated to-and-fro motion of an object about its equilibrium position.

A pendulum, a playground swing and a mass attached to a spring are common examples of oscillating systems.

A complete oscillation is made only when the object returns to its starting position while moving in the same direction in which it started.

Many beginners wrongly assume that moving from one extreme position to the other is a complete oscillation. In reality, that is only half an oscillation.

Understanding what constitutes one complete oscillation is essential because the period of an oscillating body is defined as the time taken to complete one full oscillation.
steps:
Step 1: Identify the starting position.

The pendulum starts from the left extreme position, L.

Step 2: Follow the complete motion.

The bob swings from L through the equilibrium position O to the right extreme position R. This is only half an oscillation.

Step 3: Continue the motion.

The bob then swings back from R through O until it reaches L again.

Step 4: Determine whether the starting condition has been restored.

The pendulum has returned to its original position, L, ready to repeat the same motion. Therefore, one complete oscillation has been completed.

Step 5: Compare with the options.

Option C correctly describes the complete motion.
why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is incorrect because moving from the left extreme to the equilibrium position represents only one-quarter of a complete oscillation.
Option B is incorrect because moving from one extreme position to the opposite extreme represents only half an oscillation.
Option D is incorrect because moving from the equilibrium position to one extreme and back to the equilibrium position also represents only half an oscillation.
explanation.exam_tip: Whenever a JAMB question asks for one complete oscillation, check whether the object returns to its original position and is ready to repeat the same motion. Reaching the opposite extreme alone is not enough.
explanation.final_answer: C. From L to R and back to L
explanation.simple_explanation:
Imagine a child on a playground swing.

If the swing starts from the highest point on one side, moves to the highest point on the other side and then comes back to the original side, one complete swing has been made.

Stopping at the opposite side means only half of the journey has been completed.

A pendulum behaves in exactly the same way.

question: A group of students performing a WAEC Physics practical uses a stopwatch to measure the time taken for 18 complete oscillations of a simple pendulum. The total time recorded is 27 s. What is the period of the pendulum?

explanation.question_restate: This question tests your ability to calculate the period of an oscillating body when the total time taken for several complete oscillations is known.
explanation.principle:
Before solving this question, you need to understand what the period of an oscillation means.

The period is the time taken for one complete oscillation. Since measuring the time for just one oscillation can introduce large experimental errors, physicists usually measure the time taken for many complete oscillations and then divide by the number of oscillations.

The fundamental formula for calculating the period is:

T = t/N

where:
T = period (seconds, s)
t = total time for all complete oscillations (seconds, s)
N = number of complete oscillations.

This formula is fundamental in oscillation experiments and is closely related to the frequency formula, f = 1/T, which you will study next. A larger period means each oscillation takes longer to complete, while a smaller period means the oscillations occur more quickly.
steps:
Step 1: Write down the known values.

Total time, t = 27 s
Number of complete oscillations, N = 18

Step 2: State the required quantity.

Required: Period, T

Step 3: Write the appropriate formula.

T = t/N

Step 4: Substitute the given values.

T = 27/18

Step 5: Calculate the answer.

T = 1.50 s

Step 6: Verify with the options.

Option B gives 1.50 s, so it is the correct answer.
why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A (0.67 s) is incorrect. It results from dividing the number of oscillations by the total time (18/27) instead of dividing the total time by the number of oscillations.
Option C (18 s) is incorrect because it is simply the number of oscillations, not the time taken for one oscillation.
Option D (45 s) is incorrect because it does not result from the correct application of the period formula.
explanation.misconception_alert: A common mistake is to divide the number of oscillations by the total time instead of dividing the total time by the number of oscillations. Always remember that period is the time taken for one oscillation.
explanation.exam_tip: Whenever a practical question gives the total time for several oscillations, immediately think of the formula T = t/N. This is one of the most frequently tested SHM calculations in JAMB and WAEC.
explanation.simple_explanation:
Suppose it takes 27 seconds to clap 18 complete times at a steady rhythm. To know how long one clap cycle takes, you simply share the total time equally among the 18 cycles.

In the same way, the period is the total time divided by the number of complete oscillations.

Therefore, each oscillation takes 1.50 s.

question: A Physics practical examination requires a candidate to determine the period of a simple pendulum. The candidate records that 24 complete oscillations take 36 s. What is the period of the pendulum?

explanation.question_restate: This question tests your ability to determine the period of an oscillating body from experimental measurements obtained during a Physics practical.
explanation.principle:
Before solving this question, it is important to understand why physicists measure several oscillations instead of just one.

The period of an oscillating body is the time taken for one complete oscillation.

In practical experiments, timing a single oscillation is often inaccurate because of human reaction time when starting and stopping the stopwatch. To reduce this error, the time for many complete oscillations is measured. The period is then obtained by dividing the total measured time by the number of complete oscillations.

The fundamental formula is:

T = t/N

where:

T = period (seconds, s)
t = total time for all complete oscillations (seconds, s)
N = number of complete oscillations.

This relationship is fundamental in Simple Harmonic Motion and is closely connected with the frequency formula:

f = 1/T

A longer period means each oscillation takes more time, while a shorter period means the oscillations occur more rapidly.
steps:
Step 1: Identify the known quantities.

Total time, t = 36 s
Number of complete oscillations, N = 24

Step 2: State the required quantity.

Required: Period, T

Step 3: Write the appropriate formula.

T = t/N

Step 4: Substitute the given values.

T = 36/24

Step 5: Perform the calculation.

T = 1.50 s

Step 6: Compare the calculated value with the options.

Option A is 1.50 s, so it is the correct answer.
why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B (0.67 s) is incorrect because it comes from reversing the formula and calculating 24/36 instead of 36/24.
Option C (60 s) is incorrect because it is not obtained from the period formula and is much larger than the measured total time.
Option D (24 s) is incorrect because it represents the number of oscillations, not the time for one oscillation.
explanation.misconception_alert: Students often divide the number of oscillations by the total time instead of dividing the total time by the number of oscillations. Remember that period is the time taken for one oscillation, so time must always be divided by the number of oscillations.
explanation.exam_tip: Whenever you see a stopwatch experiment involving several oscillations, immediately recall the formula T = t/N. Always check that your answer is expressed in seconds because period is a measure of time.
explanation.simple_explanation:
Imagine 24 students leaving a classroom one after another over a total time of 36 seconds. To find the average time taken for one student to leave, you divide the total time by the number of students.

The same idea applies here. Divide the total time by the number of complete oscillations to obtain the period.

Therefore, the period is 1.50 s.

question: Two children are playing on identical playground swings during the lunch break. Swing X completes one oscillation in 1.2 s, while Swing Y completes one oscillation in 1.8 s. Which statement is correct about the periods of the two swings?

options.A: Swing Y has the shorter period because it takes more time for one oscillation.
options.B: Both swings have the same period because they are identical.
options.C: Swing X has the longer period because it completes more oscillations in the same time.
options.D: Swing Y has the longer period because it takes more time to complete one oscillation.

answer_text: Swing Y has the longer period because it takes more time to complete one oscillation.

explanation.question_restate: This question tests your understanding of how to compare the periods of two oscillating systems using the time taken for one complete oscillation.
explanation.principle:
Before answering this question, it is important to understand what period means.

The period of an oscillating body is the time taken to complete one full oscillation. It is represented by the symbol T and is measured in seconds (s).

When comparing two oscillating bodies, the one with the greater period takes a longer time to complete one oscillation. Conversely, the one with the smaller period completes each oscillation more quickly.

This idea is closely related to frequency, where:

f = 1/T

Although frequency is not required to solve this question, it is useful to know that a longer period corresponds to a lower frequency, while a shorter period corresponds to a higher frequency.
steps:
Step 1: Identify the given periods.

Swing X: 1.2 s
Swing Y: 1.8 s

Step 2: Recall the meaning of period.

A larger period means more time is required for one complete oscillation.

Step 3: Compare the two values.

Since 1.8 s is greater than 1.2 s, Swing Y takes longer to complete one oscillation.

Step 4: Select the correct statement.

Therefore, Swing Y has the longer period.
why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is incorrect because taking more time for one oscillation means a longer period, not a shorter one.
Option B is incorrect because the measured periods are different. Identical swings can have different measured periods under different conditions.
Option C is incorrect because Swing X has the smaller period. Completing oscillations more quickly means a shorter period, not a longer one.
explanation.misconception_alert: Students often confuse a longer period with faster motion. In reality, a longer period means each oscillation takes more time, so the motion is slower.
explanation.exam_tip: When comparing periods, ignore unnecessary details and compare only the time taken for one complete oscillation. The larger time always corresponds to the larger period.
explanation.final_answer: D. Swing Y has the longer period because it takes more time to complete one oscillation.
explanation.simple_explanation:
Imagine two friends walking around the same playground. If one person takes 1.2 seconds to complete a lap while the other takes 1.8 seconds, the second person is taking longer for each lap.

The same idea applies to oscillations. Since Swing Y needs more time for one complete swing, it has the longer period.

question: Engineers in a school laboratory are testing a spring-mass system. During the experiment, the attached mass completes 16 complete oscillations in 20 s. What is the period of the spring-mass system?

explanation.question_restate: This question tests your ability to calculate the period of a spring-mass system from the total time taken for several complete oscillations.
explanation.principle:
Before solving this question, it is important to understand that a spring-mass system is another example of a body executing Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM). Just like a pendulum, it moves repeatedly to and fro about an equilibrium position.

The period is the time taken for one complete oscillation. In laboratory experiments, the period is usually determined by timing several complete oscillations with a stopwatch and dividing the total time by the number of oscillations. Measuring many oscillations instead of one reduces the effect of human reaction time and improves the accuracy of the result.

The fundamental formula is:

T = t/N

where:

T = period (seconds, s)
t = total time for all complete oscillations (seconds, s)
N = number of complete oscillations.

This formula is closely related to the frequency formula:

f = 1/T

A larger period means the oscillations are slower, while a smaller period means they occur more rapidly.
steps:
Step 1: Write down the known quantities.

Total time, t = 20 s
Number of complete oscillations, N = 16

Step 2: State the required quantity.

Required: Period, T

Step 3: Write the appropriate formula.

T = t/N

Step 4: Substitute the values.

T = 20/16

Step 5: Perform the calculation.

T = 1.25 s

Step 6: Verify the answer.

Option B is 1.25 s, so it is the correct answer.
why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A (0.80 s) is incorrect because it results from reversing the formula by calculating 16/20 instead of 20/16.
Option C (4.00 s) is incorrect because it does not follow from the experimental data and overestimates the period.
Option D (36.00 s) is incorrect because it is unrelated to the correct application of the period formula.
explanation.misconception_alert: A common mistake is to divide the number of oscillations by the total time. Always remember that the period is the time taken for one oscillation, so divide the total time by the number of oscillations.
explanation.exam_tip: Whenever an experiment gives the total time for several oscillations, immediately apply T = t/N. Always express the final answer in seconds because period is a measure of time.
explanation.simple_explanation:
Imagine 16 people sharing 20 seconds equally to complete one activity each. The time for one person's activity is found by dividing the total time by 16.

The same idea applies to oscillations. Divide the total time by the number of complete oscillations.

Therefore, the period of the spring-mass system is 1.25 s.
